worked_solution:
A differential equation is a d'Alembert differential equation if it can be expressed in the form

$$
y=xf({y}^{′})+g({y}^{′}),
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are differentiable functions of ${y}^{′}.$ 

In our case, we wish to transform the equation

$$
y=x{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

into a first-order linear equation for $x=x(t).$ We proceed in three steps:

**Step 1**: Substitute, and differentiate with respect to $x.$

We have the substitution

$$
t=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Substituting this into the equation gives

$$
y=x{t}^{2}+t.
$$

Differentiating both sides with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x{t}^{2}+t).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the sum and product rules and using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x{t}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(t) \\ t & ={t}^{2}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)+x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({t}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(t) \\ t & ={t}^{2}+2xt\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}+\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Isolate the derivative and take its reciprocal.

We isolate $\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}t-{t}^{2} & =2xt\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}+\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x} \\ t(1-t) & =(2xt+1)\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x} \\ \frac{t(1-t)}{2xt+1} & =\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}=\frac{t(1-t)}{2xt+1}.
$$

Therefore, by taking the reciprocal of each side, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=\frac{2xt+1}{t(1-t)}.
$$

**Step 3**: Express the derivative as a first-order linear equation.

Finally, we write this in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+P(t)x=Q(t)
$$

as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{2xt+1}{t(1-t)} \\ t(1-t)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =2xt+1 \\ t(1-t)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-2xt & =1 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-\frac{2xt}{t(1-t)} & =\frac{1}{t(1-t)} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-\frac{2x}{1-t} & =\frac{1}{t(1-t)} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{2x}{t-1} & =\frac{1}{t(1-t)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
P(t)=\frac{2}{t-1},\,Q(t)=\frac{1}{t(1-t)}.
$$
html:
A differential equation is a d'Alembert differential equation if it can be expressed in the form y=xf(y′)+g(y′), where f and g are differentiable functions of y′.

In our case, we wish to transform the equation y=x(dydx)2+dydx into a first-order linear equation for x=x(t). We proceed in three steps:

Step 1: Substitute, and differentiate with respect to x.

We have the substitution t=dydx.

Substituting this into the equation gives y=xt2+t.

Differentiating both sides with respect to x, we have ddx(y)=ddx(xt2+t).

Applying the sum and product rules and using implicit differentiation, we get dydx=ddx(xt2)+ddx(t)t=t2ddx(x)+xddx(t2)+ddx(t)t=t2+2xtdtdx+dtdx.

Step 2: Isolate the derivative and take its reciprocal.

We isolate dtdx as follows:

t−t2=2xtdtdx+dtdxt(1−t)=(2xt+1)dtdxt(1−t)2xt+1=dtdx which gives dtdx=t(1−t)2xt+1.

Therefore, by taking the reciprocal of each side, we have dxdt=2xt+1t(1−t).

Step 3: Express the derivative as a first-order linear equation.

Finally, we write this in the form dxdt+P(t)x=Q(t) as follows: dxdt=2xt+1t(1−t)t(1−t)dxdt=2xt+1t(1−t)dxdt−2xt=1dxdt−2xtt(1−t)=1t(1−t)dxdt−2x1−t=1t(1−t)dxdt+2xt−1=1t(1−t)

Therefore, we conclude that P(t)=2t−1,Q(t)=1t(1−t).
